problem: RL research on robotics is evaluated almost only in simulation; no common, publicly accessible real-world benchmark exists to track RL progress on physical robots, and earlier remote testbeds (LAGR, Robotarium, TeleWorkBench) lacked defined tasks, RL ecosystem integration or long runtime.
motivation: Community benchmarks tend to determine what gets solved, so real-world RL needs a shared physical benchmark. Hardware cost, maintenance and resets keep most researchers from real-robot experiments, so remote access behind a familiar gym API removes that barrier.
key_idea: Provide free public remote access to real robot navigation environments (and matching Gazebo simulated replicas) through the OpenAI Gym API, with a leaderboard, so RL can be benchmarked on a real robot from camera input alone.
insight: End-to-end RL (Double DQN, SAC) can learn a visual beacon-reaching navigation task directly on a real wheeled robot using only depth input and no localization, with results the authors say match simulation in similar sample complexity. Localization from an HTC Vive tracker is used only inside the environment for reward and reset, keeping the agent's observation purely visual. No ablations are reported; the evidence is only learning curves.
method: Environments: four tasks (MonolithDiscrete/Continuous and MonolithObstaclesDiscrete/Continuous) in which a Husarion Rosbot must reach a visual monolith beacon using only 320x240 RGBD camera input; sparse +1 reward within 40 cm; episodes end on success, 100 steps, or boundary contact; random start pose after each reset.

Physical setup: 3x4x2 m Moon-like enclosure with lava rock terrain, power, network, two overhead monitoring cameras; HTC Vive tracker and base stations localize the robot internally for reward computation and resets (not exposed to the agent).
Simulated replicas: Gazebo environments matching dimensions, mass, friction, reward and reset logic, with the ground as one uneven mesh; available in Docker containers for sim-to-real research.

System architecture: Python client library, gym server for resource management and control, ROS action server to the robot, with a time-booking system and leaderboard; each step takes ~2 s fixed plus latency (up to 4 s).
Gym API: drop-in gym.make('OffWorldMonolithDiscreteReal-v0') vs the Sim variant, with selectable channel type (depth only etc.).
Baselines: Double DQN (3381 params, depth 320x240, replay 25k, eps 0.9 to 0.1 over 40k steps) and SAC (84x84 depth, 757,236 params, batch 1024, replay 500k) on discrete; SAC on continuous.

setting.backbone: Small CNN + FC networks trained from scratch (Double DQN, Soft Actor-Critic)
setting.training_data: Online RL on the real robot in MonolithReal environment (sparse reward); no extra data
setting.observation: depth channel only of RGBD camera (320x240 for DDQN, 84x84 for SAC); no localization
setting.action_space: discrete: left/right/forward/backward with 2 s step; or continuous linear and angular velocities
setting.privileged: none for the agent (HTC Vive localization used only by the environment for reward/reset)

numbers_note: Results only given as learning curves in a figure (Fig. 2); no numeric metrics reported.
results: Double DQN and SAC learn to reach the beacon in the real discrete environment, and SAC also does so in the continuous variant, from depth alone. Only learning curves are shown, with no numeric comparison; the authors claim similar sample complexity in simulation.
limitations: Only one of the four environments (MonolithReal, without obstacles) is benchmarked, and only with learning curves and no quantitative metrics
Slow real-time steps (2-4 s), resets and limited robot availability restrict throughput and scalability; sparse reward relies on external tracking
Simple task; simulation results and sim-to-real transfer not reported
